messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marcus, a 35-year-old European-American single male and special education teacher, has been struggling with the aftermath of a mugging that occurred three months ago. The traumatic event began when Marcus was walking home late one evening after work. A group of men surrounded him on an empty street, shouting at him to hand over his wallet. As Marcus tried to comply, they attacked him, causing severe neck pain and leaving him feeling helpless and terrified. Since the mugging, Marcus has been hyper-aware of any signs that might remind him of the attack. The sound of shouting in his neighborhood or on television triggers vivid memories, and he often finds himself reliving the experience as if it were happening again. For example, during a school fire drill at work, Marcus was overwhelmed by shouting and found himself paralyzed with fear, convinced the attackers had returned. This triggered intense rage and guilt as he remembers the helplessness of that night. Marcus’s negative appraisals exacerbate his symptoms. He believes that if someone else were in his position, they would have handled it better or avoided such a situation altogether. These thoughts contribute to his constant state of hypervigilance, making him feel inadequate and unable to relax even when he knows he is safe. This constant tension manifests physically; Marcus frequently checks for exits upon entering any building or room, fearing that another attack could happen at any moment. When Marcus recalls the event, it feels like he is reliving every detail with photographic clarity. The memory of the attackers’ faces and their voices shouting at him bring back intense emotions, including guilt over not being able to fight back more effectively. These memories fuel his hypervigilance and reinforce his belief that he cannot trust others or protect himself. The fear of another attack has permeated Marcus’s daily life. He avoids going out alone after dark and hesitates to engage in activities he once enjoyed, such as attending school events or meeting friends for drinks. The guilt over not handling the situation better and the rage at his attackers have made it difficult for him to focus on work or social interactions. What frightens Marcus most is the possibility of another attack and the fear that he will be unable to protect himself again. He has noticed that this constant threat monitoring has affected his ability to teach effectively, as he finds it hard to concentrate on lessons when he is preoccupied with potential dangers. This concern about his job performance only adds to his sense of inadequacy. The accumulation of these experiences and the fear of another attack have finally pushed Marcus to seek help. He hopes that therapy can provide him with strategies to cope with the overwhelming memories and fears, allowing him to regain a sense of control over his life and return to being an effective teacher.
